prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its glucose-dependent and appetite-regulating actions that made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The case rests on a physiological discovery that is specific and mechanistically clear: GLP-1 is a proglucagon-derived incretin with glucose-dependent insulinotropic, satiety and gastric-emptying actions in humans. It has been independently confirmed for two decades, led to several approved drug classes, and now carries randomized outcome evidence in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. Few candidates combine a hormone-physiology core with clinical effect on this scale. I still favour the three discovery-side scientists (Holst for human GLP-1 physiology, Drucker for receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, Mojsov for identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide), which keeps the prize anchored in physiology as the Medicine prize is meant to be.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener, who is not on the credited list, is disputed in the literature and I cannot settle it from the supplied names. Leaving out Knudsen, whose liraglutide and semaglutide work produced the drugs patients actually take, risks a prize that appears to honour the idea but not the medicine. A prize this prominent could also be read as late rather than urgent, and long-term safety beyond metabolic disease is still being defined. If the committee judged the discovery-side credit too contested, the cleaner fallback is a different candidate, not a hurried reshuffle of names.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Mojsov as the most contested name and valuing the long-acting analogue design as part of a physiology-to-medicine arc.
responses.response: I take the point that Mojsov's claim is the most disputed and that Knudsen's analogue design is what turned the physiology into medicine. But the Prize has mostly honoured the discovery that enabled a therapy, and the enabling step here is the identification of the active peptide and its insulinotropic action. Drug engineering of acylated analogues builds on that discovery. If the committee decides the priority dispute over the peptide cannot be resolved, Knudsen would be a defensible substitute for Mojsov. I do not think she should be preferred over her on the evidence we have been given.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked GLP-1 first as a complete arc from hormone biology to drugs, and flagged that the priority question around Mojsov versus other laboratories needs careful review. He also ranked TNF blockade fourth.
responses.response: I agree that the Mojsov priority review is the key open step and that we should not name her on the strength of recollection alone. On TNF blockade, I see the same strengths he does, but I would still keep it as an alternative rather than the lead. It is a clinical-translation prize resting on Feldmann and Maini, and the underlying TNF biology (Old, Cerami, Beutler) sits outside the credited names. That makes its attribution less complete than I would like, even though I work in this field and should discount any pull toward it.

responses.point: Perlmann put the unfolded protein response second, citing conceptual originality and a clean Walter and Mori pair, with cGAS-STING third.
responses.response: I share his respect for the mechanistic clarity of the UPR and the clean attribution to Walter and Mori; of the basic-science candidates it is the best defined. Where I differ is that the medical connection is still largely indirect, whereas the committee can point to patient outcomes for CAR-T cells. I would not put it above them as a lead. I also note that the cGAS-STING pathway, which he ranks third, has no approved therapy yet, so it is the earlier of the two on the clinical side even though the mechanism is solid.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked optogenetics second as a general method that changed experimental practice, while acknowledging that any trio leaves out major contributors among six credited names.
responses.response: I accept that optogenetics is among the most influential tools of the last twenty years. My reservation is the one he states himself: the six credited names do not fit within three places, and the dispute over priority among the neuronal demonstrations (Boyden, Deisseroth, Miesenboeck, Bamberg) could not be resolved by us without an injustice to someone. For a prize that is a clean physiological discovery, I find the GLP-1 attribution problem more manageable than the optogenetics one, so I place it lower than he does.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution can be credited in preference to others (Habener is not on the list) without a priority review I cannot do from the supplied material.
Whether the committee prefers a physiology-only prize or one that includes the drug-development line (Knudsen).
How to weigh a mature, arguably overdue clinical-translation candidate (TNF blockade, CAR-T) against the basic-science candidates if GLP-1 attribution stalls.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred GLP-1 configuration. TNF blockade (B006) lies in my own field of rheumatology, and I mention it only as an alternative; my recorded co-authors (Kuchroo, Sonesson) and my Bergen affiliation do not connect me to any named candidate, and I infer no personal ties from them.
